catalog_quote: Since there is such strong evidence of a central cordilleran pattern of pitch utilisation in word-tone systems, with a ‘spillover’ of pitch-accent to the south, it is surprising that Ross did not examine the languages to the north of the main range. The languages are not part of the TNG family, but are tonal with tone bearing a high contrastive load. Examples of such languages include Yetfa and Lepki, immediately north of, and in contact with, Mek languages from the highlands, and further away Kaure. See Map 3 for a complete picture of tonal patterns in New Guinea.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (21 pp., no text layer; the PDF's metadata gives the Producer DocuCentre-II C2200, i.e. a scanner). The scanned page file ocr2005/ contains footnote 4 word for word as quoted ("Since there is such strong evidence of a central cordilleran pattern of pitch utilisation in word-tone systems.. The languages are not part of the TNG family, but are tonal with tone bearing a high contrastive load. Examples of such languages include Yetfa and Lepki, immediately north of, and in contact with, Mek languages from the highlands, and further away Kaure. See Map 3 for a complete picture of tonal patterns in New Guinea."). I rendered PDF page 4 to PNG and read the footnote on the image: identical to…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lepki is classed as a tone language in which tone carries a high contrastive (lexical) load; no word-stress rule is stated and no stress position is given. This is a one-sentence areal-typological classification resting on the author's own hurriedly collected 1998 wordlist, not a phonological description.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement groups Lepki with Yetfa (and Kaure) as non-TNG tonal languages north of the central range.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone implied ('tone bearing a high contrastive load'); no discussion of the tone-bearing unit, tone inventory, or word vs phrase domain. The claim is first-hand only in the sense that Donohue collected the Lepki wordlist himself; the paper is an areal survey of tone in New Guinea, not a description of Lepki. Ethnologue 18 (2015) independently lists Lepki as 'tonal' with no source, and Foley 2018: 466 (snippet only) repeats 'tonal' for the Lepki family.
new_statements.identity_note: Lepki proper [lpe], lepk1238, Sobger/Sogber River, Pegunungan Bintang (Andersen's 'Lepki people of Sogber River'; Ethnologue 'Lepki'). Donohue's footnote groups Lepki with its neighbour Yetfa (yetf1238) in one sentence; Andersen 2007 (p. 7) notes small north/south internal differences 'that may indicate two possible dialects' but names none. Sister languages Murkim (murk1238) and Kembra (kemb1250) are in the same no-description state.
